newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr sits back for well earned rest.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr sits back for well earned rest.

text.p: The Australian dollar took a small step back Tuesday as its two week upward charge finally rebounded from a stiff chart barrier at 78 cents.

Traders said sales came from U.S. and Japanese names as recent gains, 2-1/2 cents in total, proved too tempting for some holders who took profits. A large AUD/CAD sell order was also reported, for much the same reason, and combined to drag the currency back to support atop US$0.7750.
Scope was seen for a deeper retracement to US$0.7720, but good bids were believed to be crowded there which should protect key US$0.7680 bulwark and allow at least one more tilt higher.
By 4.55 pm (0555 GMT) the local dollar had sat back at US$0.7758/63 from an early US$0.7773/78 and US$0.7770/75 late here Monday.

It had briefly touched 78 cents offshore on the back of U.K. and Swiss bank demand, so fulfilling a technical target of a 38 percent retracement of the entire decline from US$0.8212 in early December to US$0.7550 on February 12.

Chart watchers said a period of consolidation often followed such a development, but the bias would remain upward as long as US$0.7680 stayed intact. Clearing 78 would likely trigger a stop-loss squeeze to US$0.7850 and open the way to 80 cents.
The currency also lost ground on the crosses where it was burdened with a waning US$/yen as welll as selling out of Tokyo as investors there took profits on Australian bond holdings.

That dragged it down to 94.71/81 yen from 95.26/36 late Monday, while the U.S. dollar slipped to 122.10 yen from 122.60. In trade weighted terms the local currency eased to 59.3 from a previous 59.5 close.

Traders expected the softness to be short-lived given that the A$'s relatively high, and increasing, yield offered a compelling reason for investors in low rate countries like Japan and Germany to hold the currency.
Money market rates here has risen sharply in the last couple of weeks as signs of economic pick-up encouraged the Reserve Bank to rule out another rate cut, at least for the time being.
The seachange in sentiment was clear in the futures market which had abandoned all hope of a cut in March and was now actually pricing in a tightening before year-end.
The December 90-day bank bill contract had tumbled to 93.32 indicating the market was betting on official rates being around 6.68 percent then from 6.00 percent now.
Whether that aggressive outlook was actually justified might be easier to assess once data on wages were released this week.
The RBA warned on wages growth just a week ago so any sign of upward pressure in the data would tend to support the dollar.
The Department of Industrial Relations December quarter report on wage trends in enterprise bargaining is due Wednesday.

Wage rises in the September quarter slowed to 4.8 percent across the economy and to 5.3 percent for private sector pay deals alone, compared to 5.3 and 6.1 percent respectively in Q2. The RBA has often stated that wage growth of more than 4.5-5.0 percent was incompatible with maintaining underlying inflation in its 2-3 percent target band.

On Thursday, final average weekly earnings figures (AWOTE) for the November quarter are due which originally showed a higher than expected 1.2 percent gain on the quarter and 3.9 percent rise year-on-year.
Analysts noted the data from the previous two quarters were revised up in their final release.
The data will also include a breakdown between public and private sector wages, which will be important since analysts felt the public sector may have biased up the overall AWOTE.
